fields.Front: Why do we use layering to organize networks? (two reasons from the slides)
fields.Back: 1) Explicit structure allows identification of and relationships among a complex system's pieces (a layered reference model for discussion). 2) Modularization eases maintenance and updating: a change in one layer's service implementation is transparent to the rest of the system.

fields.Front: In the air-travel analogy, what are the five layers/services?
fields.Back: Ticketing service, baggage service, gate service, runway (takeoff/landing) service, and airplane routing service.

fields.Front: How does each layer implement its service?
fields.Back: Via its own internal-layer actions, and by relying on the services provided by the layer below it.

fields.Text: Each layer implements a service via its own {{c1::internal-layer actions}} and by relying on services provided by the {{c2::layer below}}.

fields.Front: Give a potential drawback of layering ('layering considered harmful').
fields.Back: Layers may duplicate functionality (e.g., error recovery both per-link and end-to-end), or one layer may need information available only in another layer, violating separation.

fields.Front: List the five layers of the Internet protocol stack, top to bottom.
Application layer: role and example protocols.
fields.Back: Supports network applications. Examples: HTTP, SMTP, IMAP (also DNS). Its packet is a message.

fields.Front: Transport layer: role and example protocols.
fields.Back: Process-to-process data transfer. Examples: TCP (connection-oriented, reliable, flow and congestion control) and UDP (connectionless, no-frills). Its packet is a segment.

fields.Front: Network layer: role and example protocols.
fields.Back: Routing of datagrams from source host to destination host. Examples: IP and routing protocols. Its packet is a datagram.

fields.Front: Link layer: role and example protocols.
fields.Back: Data transfer between neighbouring network elements (one hop). Examples: Ethernet, 802.11 (WiFi), PPP. Its packet is a frame.

fields.Text: The physical layer moves the individual {{c1::bits 'on the wire'}} from one node to the next; its protocol depends on the medium.
Application-layer protocols include {{c1::HTTP, SMTP, IMAP}}; transport: {{c2::TCP, UDP}}; network: {{c3::IP, routing protocols}}; link: {{c4::Ethernet, 802.11 (WiFi), PPP}}.

fields.Front: Name the packet (PDU) at each layer: application, transport, network, link.
fields.Back: Message (application), segment (transport), datagram (network), frame (link). The physical layer carries bits.

fields.Text: PDU names: application = {{c1::message}}, transport = {{c2::segment}}, network = {{c3::datagram}}, link = {{c4::frame}}.

fields.Front: Which layers are TCP, IP, HTTP, Ethernet, and UDP in?
fields.Back: TCP: transport. IP: network. HTTP: application. Ethernet: link. UDP: transport.

fields.Front: How many layers does the ISO/OSI reference model have, and which two are not in the Internet stack?
fields.Back: Seven. The presentation layer (data interpretation: encryption, compression, machine conventions) and the session layer (delimiting, synchronization, checkpointing/recovery) sit between application and transport; the Internet leaves these to the application.

fields.Text: OSI 7-layer model, top to bottom: application, {{c1::presentation}}, {{c2::session}}, transport, network, {{c3::data link}}, physical.
